items.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013
items.q: control over the top end of his instrument. And that’s something that I wanted to do.

ctx.x: I think I probably did. I listened to a lot of baritone players when I was a kid, on recordings. And for a large part they sounded clunky and clumsy and certain parts of the instrument were strong and certain parts were weak. And I was listening primarily to tenor players and alto players, people like Lester Young, who had shaped his sound on a C melody saxophone sound that Frankie Trumbauer had. So his sound was lighter. And then Stan Getz, who had listened to alto players when he first played, early on, when he…

control over the top end of his instrument. And that’s something that I wanted to do. And because I also — I liked Cannonball Adderley. I wanted to bring that same concept. I figured the guy’s got the same amount of fingers and the same amount of keys, why can’t I do that on the baritone? And so a lot of what I did is in the upper register and going into harmonics. I want it to be as clean as the rest of the sound of the instrument. So you have a pyramid effect. The top end of the horn is like this and the bottom…
Did you ever consider playing the tenor?
